vignette:
Ravi was 58 when he finally came to treatment, a married South Asian American product manager who had spent most of his adult life building a career in structured, high-responsibility work. He described the assault that marked his life in spare, careful language, as though too much detail would bring it too close. Years earlier, while traveling, he had been taken and tortured by men in uniform. What stayed with him was not only the physical pain but the way authority, weapons, and commands became fused with terror in a way he could not shake. He remembered being forced to listen to rapid, incomprehensible chatter around him, unable to tell what was being said or what would happen next, and he had felt then that his body had betrayed him by going dizzy and lightheaded while he was still fully aware of everything. Those moments lodged in memory with a sharpness that still surprised him. Even now, a burst of sirens on the street could pull him back into that helpless state, and the sound of overlapping, unintelligible conversation in a crowded room could make him tense immediately, as if the world around him had become hostile and unreadable again.

In the months and years that followed, Ravi’s daily life narrowed around a series of careful rules. He had come to avoid anything that might be stressful, not because he thought stress was unpleasant, but because he felt he could not afford to be thrown off balance. At work, where his role as a product manager depended on meetings, deadlines, and constant problem-solving, he began to organize his days around keeping himself as steady as possible. He tried to steer clear of situations he anticipated would raise his heart rate or leave him feeling exposed. He also watched his body with unusual vigilance. He checked repeatedly for signs of danger or injury, scanning for any subtle shift that might mean something was wrong with him. When he felt even slightly dizzy, his attention narrowed completely. That sensation had become especially potent for him because it echoed the helpless lightheadedness he had experienced during the torture, and he could not stop himself from testing whether his hands were steady or his breathing was normal. He did this at his desk, in the restroom at work, and sometimes in the car before going into the office, making sure he was not missing some internal warning.

Uniforms and weapons remained especially hard for him to tolerate. He made deliberate choices about where he went and what he watched, steering away from military or police uniforms whenever he could. If he saw an officer in the lobby of his building or on the sidewalk near his office, his attention snapped to the weapon first, then to the posture, the authority, the possibility of being ordered or cornered. He did not say this out loud, but his body reacted as if the event could begin again without warning. He had become so used to scanning that he rarely noticed the effort it took to keep himself composed. What frightened him most was how quickly he could become alert again, even in places that were objectively safe. At night he often woke to check whether he was safe, sometimes sitting upright in the dark and listening before he would let himself lie back down. He could not fully relax even in his own bed, and his wife noticed that he slept lightly and turned at the slightest sound. When she touched him unexpectedly, even in an ordinary gesture of affection, he reacted with alarm before he could think. He would stiffen, inhale sharply, and then feel embarrassed at having startled so easily.

Over time, Ravi’s view of other people changed as well. He had come to believe that people could not be trusted, a conviction shaped by what he had endured and reinforced by the feeling that no one had protected him when it mattered. He spoke with a heavy sense that there was something about him that had made the event happen, as if some personal flaw or weakness had made him the kind of person who could be selected and broken. Alongside this sat a bleak expectation that nothing good could happen to him anymore. He did not describe this as dramatic despair; instead, it came through in the flat way he talked about the future, as if positive outcomes were for other people. His marriage remained intact, and his wife had stayed beside him, but he had become more guarded and less spontaneous, and he often kept his fears to himself because he did not trust that others would understand them or handle them well. At work, the cumulative effect was that he was less at ease in meetings and more exhausted by the end of the day, not only from the demands of the job but from the constant effort of monitoring himself and the environment.

He sought help now because the pattern had become hard to ignore. The sirens outside his office, the sudden dizziness in a crowded corridor, the involuntary flinch when his wife reached for his shoulder in the kitchen, and the repeated nighttime checks had begun to feel like the life he was living rather than isolated moments. He came because he was tired of moving through the world as if danger were always one sound, one touch, or one uniform away. What he hoped for was not to forget what had happened, but to feel less trapped by it, and what he feared most was that the rest of his life would continue to be organized around vigilance, suspicion, and the sense that safety would never fully belong to him again.
